L11: ## GISTEMP GMSTA Analysis Project
L12: ### Global Mean Surface Temperature Anomaly Predictions
L13: This page shows various estimates of the current and next years' annual Global Mean Surface Temperature (GMST) anomaly for the GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP) v4 dataset, calculated with respect to the pre-industrial period 1850-1900.
L14: Conducted in partnership with the cite7†International Research Institute for Climate and Society†iri.columbia.edu (IRI) at Columbia University's Center for Climate Systems Research (CCSR), GMST anomaly predictions are generated from on a combination of North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME) forecast outputs, historical and projected December, January, February (DJF) El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) magnitudes, and a Year-to-Date (YTD) Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) bivariate regression model.
L15: The results are presented as a comparison of the different predictive methods, along with their associated confidence intervals. We provide an explanation of our methods and data sources, as well as a link to download the numerical prediction values shown in the plot below (Figure 1).
L16: Figure 1: A comparison of GMST anomaly predictions for 2026 and 2027 based on NMME model outputs, historical and projected DJF ENSO magnitudes, and a YTD OLS bivariate linear regression. Data point error bars are prediction intervals and timeseries line shading represents confidence intervals, all within 95% certainty.
L17: #### Prediction Downloads
L18: 
L19: You can download numerical GMST anomaly prediction values, and their corresponding uncertainty estimates, from the plot above cite8†as a CSV file here. (1 KB CSV file)
L20: 
L21: #### Methodologies and Sources
L22: 
L23: The anomaly with respect to 1850-1900 is calculated using the GISTEMP anomaly for 1880-1900, adjusted by the average of five other records (NOAA, HadCRUT5, Berkeley Earth, DCENT and China MST) to match the 1850-1900 period.
L24: ##### NMME Predictions
L25: The North American Multi-Model Ensemble (NMME) is a collaborative project that combines the outputs of multiple state-of-the-art computer climate models, running in the United States and Canada, to improve the accuracy of seasonal and interannual climate predictions. Early each month, real-time configurations are used to generate temperature predictions for the upcoming 12-months. Because of this, rest-of-the-year temperature predictions tend to increase in accuracy with each passing month.
L26: In this analysis, four NMME models are used to generate annual mean GMST anomaly predictions for this year. Those models are COLA-CCSM4, COLA-CESM1, CanESM5, and GEM5.2-NEMO. The predictions for each model are calculated by combining GISTEMPv4 anomalies for the observed portion of this year with the latest NMME rest-of-year forecast to calculate the full-year anomaly.
L27: NMME estimates are based on true air surface temperatures, whereas GISTEMP uses a conditional blend of air surface and sea surface temperatures. The confidence intervals around the NMME data represent the typical uncertainty spread for predictions released in the same issue month, based on historical accuracy.
L28: ##### Historical DJF ENSO Prediction
L29: The Historical ENSO predictive model was developed through sequential residual fitting. This is an iterative process where statistical model residuals are used as dependent inputs in subsequent statistical models to improve accuracy. In this case, we used the Locally Estimated Scatterplot Smoothing (LOESS) method to build a local polynomial regression modeling smoothed annual GMST anomalies using data from GISTEMP v4.
L30: Then, we developed an OLS bivariate linear regression to model the relationship between LOESS residuals and historical DJF Niño 3.4 Sea Surface Temperature (SST) indices. We then constructed a final bivariate linear regression model, using LOESS GMST anomaly predictions + OLS residual predictions to explain observed historical GMST anomalies.
L31: Using the latest DJF Niño 3.4 SST index as an input within that final bivariate linear regression model, we can predict what the annual GMST anomaly of this year will be.
L32: ##### Year-To-Date Prediction
L33: 
L34: The YTD predictive model is an OLS bivariate linear regression that models the effect of historical YTD GMST anomalies on historical annual GMST anomalies. YTD values are calculated as the average of observed monthly GMST anomalies from the beginning of the year to the current month. Using the OLS bivariate model and the current YTD GMST anomaly, we can extrapolate what this year's annual GMST anomaly will be.
L35: ##### Projected DJF ENSO Prediction
L36: The Future ENSO predictive model can be thought of as an extension of the historical ENSO predictive model, using its final bivariate linear regression to generate a prediction of what the annual GMST anomaly will be for next year. In this case, the previously developed OLS bivariate regression model is used to generate a prediction of residuals based on CCSR/IRI predictions of the upcoming DJF ENSO magnitude.
L37: We have chosen to use their predicted DJF dynamical mean and standard deviation for our calculations. Then, the previously developed LOESS polynomial regression model is used to extrapolate an annual GMST anomaly prediction for next year. Ultimately, those values are input as independent and dependent variables, respectively, to predict what the actual annual GMST anomaly will be next year.
L38: #### Publication Notes
L39: 
L40: We are providing these estimates as a public service given the interest in the topic and frequent requests we get for this information. Updates to this page will be made on a monthly basis as the source data files get updated, usually by the middle of the month. We are working on a technical paper to be submitted on the verification and calibration of these estimates.

L12: ENSO Diagnostic Discussion
L13: EL NIÑO/SOUTHERN OSCILLATION (ENSO)
L14: DIAGNOSTIC DISCUSSION
L15: issued by
L16: CLIMATE PREDICTION CENTER/NCEP/NWS
L17: 10 September 2026
L18: 
L19: ENSO Alert System Status: cite13†El Niño Advisory L20: Synopsis:  El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27. El Niño strengthened further over the past month, with sea surface temperature anomalies exceeding +3.0°C in the eastern equatorial Pacific cite14†[Fig. 1] . Except for the Niño-4 index, which decreased to +0.1°C in August, values in the other Niño indices increased, reaching +1.8°C in Niño-3.4, +2.5°C in Niño-3, and +3.4°C in Niño-1+2 cite15†[Fig. 2] .
L21: The equatorial subsurface temperature index (average from 180°-100°W) remained steady during August cite16†[Fig. 3] , reflecting a deeper-than-average thermocline cite17†[Fig. 4] . Subsurface temperatures continued to be significantly above average, with widespread anomalies in excess of +10.0°C at depth. Low-level westerly wind anomalies and upper-level easterly wind anomalies extended from the western to the east-central equatorial Pacific.
L22: Enhanced convection and rainfall persisted from the central to the eastern Pacific, while anomalies remained suppressed over Indonesia cite18†[Fig. 5] . The traditional and equatorial Southern Oscillation indices remained negative. Collectively, the coupled ocean-atmosphere system reflected a strengthening El Niño. The cite19†CPC Official ENSO outlook , which synthesizes multiple models from North America and abroad, indicates El Niño will continue to strengthen through the end of the year cite20†[Figs.
L23: 6 cite21†-7 cite22†-8] . During the October-December 2026 season, there is a 75% chance of a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950 (+2.5°C or more for a cite23†3-month RONI value ). With an event of this magnitude, the chances of experiencing impacts consistent with El Niño are larger, though not guaranteed (see cite24†CPC outlooks for probabilities of seasonal anomalies).
L24: In summary, El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27. This discussion is a consolidated effort of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), NOAA's National Weather Service, and their funded institutions. Oceanic and atmospheric conditions are updated weekly on the Climate Prediction Center web site (cite25†El Niño/La Niña Current Conditions and Expert Discussions ).
L25: A probabilistic strength forecast is cite26†available here†cpc.ncep.noaa.gov . The next ENSO Diagnostics Discussion is scheduled for 8 October 2026.
L26: To receive an e-mail notification when the monthly ENSO Diagnostic Discussions are released, please send an e-mail message to: ncep.list.enso-update@noaa.gov.

L36: ## Measles cases in 2026
L37: ### Resources for Communities with a Measles Outbreak:
L38: 
L39:   * cite14†Sample Community Letter About Measles L40:   * cite15†Be Ready for Measles Toolkit L41:   * cite16†There's a Current Outbreak of Measles L42:   * cite17†Do You Think Your Child Has Measles? L43: As of September 17, 2026, 3,471 confirmed* measles cases were reported in the United States in 2026.
L44: Among these, 3,454 measles cases were reported by 47 jurisdictions: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, District of Columbia, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York City, New York State, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.
L45: A total of 17 measles cases were reported among international visitors to the United States.
L46: There have been 39 new outbreaks** reported in 2026, and 95% of confirmed cases (3,296 of 3,471) are outbreak-associated (1,920 from outbreaks starting in 2026 and 1,376 from outbreaks that started in 2025).
L47: For the full year of 2025, a total of 2,289 confirmed* measles cases were reported in the United States.
L48: Among these, 2,263 measles cases were reported by 45 jurisdictions: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York City, New York State, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.
L49: A total of 26 measles cases were reported among international visitors to the United States.
L50: There were 48 outbreaks** reported in 2025, and 90% of confirmed cases (2,066 of 2,289) were outbreak-associated. For comparison, 16 outbreaks were reported during 2024 and 69% of cases (198 of 285) were outbreak-associated.
L51: 
L52: *CDC is aware of probable measles cases being reported by jurisdictions. However, the data on this page only includes cite18†confirmed cases†ndc.services.cdc.gov jurisdictions have notified to CDC.
L53: **CDC reports the cumulative number of measles outbreaks (defined as 3 or more related cases) that have occurred this year in the U.S.; states have the most up-to-date information about cases and outbreaks in their jurisdictions.
